titre: Valladolid, 1550: A Debate on the Indians' Humanity, Without a Verdict
accroche: In 1550, Charles V convened a debate to judge whether the conquest of the Americas was just. The deliberations lasted months without a verdict.
contenu_vulgarise:
In August 1550, the Dominican friar Bartolomé de Las Casas and the humanist Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda appear before some fifteen theologians and jurists gathered at the Colegio de San Gregorio, in Valladolid. That same year, Emperor Charles V had suspended the granting of new conquest licenses in the Americas, so that this commission could settle a question simple in appearance: is the war waged against the Indigenous peoples just?

## Two Readings of Aristotle

Sepúlveda builds his argument on Aristotle: some peoples, he says, are born incapable of governing themselves and fall into the category of “natural slaves,” whom more civilized masters have the right to subdue. He adds grounds drawn from the law of just war: punishing cannibalism, human sacrifice and idolatry, and clearing the way for evangelization by first pacifying the ground.

Las Casas answers on the same philosophical ground rather than sidestepping it: the Aristotelian category of the “barbarian” does not apply to the peoples of the Americas, whose social organization, laws and cities he has seen up close. In Scripture, he finds only a single precedent for religiously justified war, against certain Canaanite peoples, and refuses to extend it to all non-Christians. Only peaceful conversion, he argues, truly converts: a soul won over by threat remains a soul that has not believed.

Sepúlveda submits twelve rebuttals to Las Casas's arguments; Las Casas answers them point by point. The Dominican Domingo de Soto, tasked with summarizing the debates for the commission, draws no single conclusion from them: the deliberations stretch over several months, between the summer of 1550 and the spring of 1551, without any collective vote ever being recorded. Only the personal opinion of one of the judges, Doctor Anaya, survives: he allows the conquest, but only if it benefits the Indians and not the gold drawn from them.

## A Debate Without a Verdict, Which Still Settles Something

For lack of an official decision, the two men each leave declaring themselves the winner. Sepúlveda publishes his arguments; Las Casas continues, until his death in 1566, a body of work devoted to documenting the violence of the conquest. On the ground, nothing changes immediately: colonists keep reducing Indigenous populations to servitude, and the suspension of conquest licenses is lifted.

What Valladolid actually settled is not the question it was asked. It is the fact, new in Europe, that a colonial power agreed to submit the legitimacy of its own conquest to an adversarial debate before judges who were not the conquerors themselves. No court, no king had ever before formally organized a discussion of the rights of a people just subdued by arms. The absence of a verdict does not erase this novelty: it makes it, if anything, more visible, as if an embarrassing question asked aloud mattered more than the answer one refuses to give it.

repere.texte: Sepúlveda submits twelve rebuttals to Las Casas's arguments before the Valladolid commission (1550-1551); the Dominican Domingo de Soto summarizes the debates, but no collective verdict is ever recorded, and each side later declares itself the winner.

carte.punch: In 1550, Charles V opens a debate on the conquest of the Americas that will never reach a verdict.
carte.idee: Las Casas and Sepúlveda face off before a commission of theologians in Valladolid, over the humanity of Indigenous peoples and the legitimacy of conquest. Twelve rebuttals later, no collective verdict is reached: each side calls itself the winner.

quiz.question: Why does the Valladolid debate (1550-1551) end without an official verdict?
choix: Because the commission deliberates without ever recording a collective vote, and each side later declares itself the winner
Because Charles V cuts the debate short before Las Casas can answer Sepúlveda's twelve rebuttals
Because Las Casas withdraws from the debate after the first session, judging the commission won over by Sepúlveda
Because the pope annuls the commission before it can deliver its conclusions
quiz.explication: The commission deliberates for months without ever recording a collective vote; Charles V does not rule either, so Las Casas and Sepúlveda each later declare themselves the winner, for lack of a written decision to contradict them.
